name: Cut the repeat
rule: If two words or phrases mean the same thing, one of them has to go. The test calls this redundancy, and the shortest version that keeps the meaning wins.
trick: Cover the suspicious phrase. If the sentence means exactly the same thing without it, delete it.

examples.text: She returned back to the start.

another.text: "I went back and returned home" says "back" twice, because "returned" already means back. Watch for pairs that mean the same thing: "end result," "each and every," "tiny little." One of the two words is just taking up space.
another.example:
"She returned back home." → "She returned home."
"The end result" → "The result"

questions.why: Twins are always two. "Two twins" repeats.

options: The results were unexpected and surprising.
questions.why: Unexpected and surprising mean the same thing. Keep one.

name: Shorter is better
rule: When two answers mean the same thing, the shorter one is almost always correct. Extra words that add no meaning are wrong.
trick: Among the choices that are grammatically correct and mean the same, pick the shortest. Long phrases like "due to the fact that" are usually one word in disguise: "because."

examples.text: Due to the fact that it rained, we stayed in.
Because it rained, we stayed in.

another.text: Pretend every word costs a dollar. "At this point in time" costs five dollars. "Now" costs one and says the same thing. The test always wants the cheap sentence, as long as it means the same thing.
another.example:
"in the event that" ($4) → "if" ($1)
"has the ability to" ($4) → "can" ($1)

options: She has the ability to speak three languages.
A large number of students walk to school.

name: The precise word
rule: Pick the word that says exactly what the sentence needs: not too strong, not too weak, and the right meaning for the context.
trick: Read the whole sentence for clues about size, feeling, or direction. Then ask which choice matches those clues most exactly.

examples.text: The tiny crack grew into a gap you could fit a hand through.
examples.note: Tiny matches "grew into," which needs a small start.

examples.text: The enormous crack grew into a gap you could fit a hand through.
examples.note: Enormous is too strong for something that then grows to hand-sized.

another.text: Words come in sizes, like small, medium, large. Damp, wet, soaked. Warm, hot, burning. The sentence tells you what size you need. A kid who dropped their ice cream is sad. A kid whose dog ran away is heartbroken. Pick the size that fits.
another.example:
Dropped ice cream → sad
Dog ran away → heartbroken
Same feeling, different sizes

questions.blank: After a week without rain, the soil was __ and cracked.
questions.why: No rain and cracked soil means dry. Damp and soaked go the wrong direction.

questions.blank: The storm caused __ damage: a few shingles and one broken window.
questions.why: A few shingles and a window is minor. The colon lists the clue.

name: Matching the tone
rule: A word has to fit the voice of the passage around it. A formal report doesn't say "super cool," and a casual story doesn't say "henceforth."
trick: Read the sentence before and after. If they sound like a textbook, pick the textbook word. If they sound like a friend talking, pick the friendly word.

examples.text: The committee reviewed the budget and decided the numbers were totally bogus.
The committee reviewed the budget and decided the numbers were inaccurate.

another.text: Think about clothes. You don't wear a swimsuit to a wedding or a tuxedo to the pool. Words are the same. A serious report doesn't say "super cool," and a fun story doesn't say "henceforth." Look at what the other words are wearing and match them.
another.example:
Serious passage: wrong → incorrect
Fun passage: incorrect → wrong

questions.blank: The study's authors __ that the drug reduced symptoms in most patients.
questions.why: "Study's authors" and "patients" are formal. "Concluded" matches; "reckon" and "figure" are slang.

questions.blank: My little brother __ his vegetables into his napkin when Mom wasn't looking.
questions.why: A family story about a little brother is casual. "Stuffed" fits; the other two sound like a shipping manifest.

name: Should this sentence be added?
sub: Only if it does a job for the paragraph
rule: A sentence belongs in a paragraph only if it supports the paragraph's main point. Interesting but off-topic is still off-topic.
trick: Name the paragraph's point in a few words. Then ask whether the new sentence helps make that point. If it's about something else, the answer is no, even if it's true.
passage: Paragraph: Beavers reshape rivers. Their dams slow the water, which creates ponds, and the ponds become homes for fish, frogs, and birds.

examples.text: Add: "A single dam can flood several acres."
Add: "Beavers have orange teeth because of iron in the enamel."
examples.note: Cool fact, nothing to do with rivers.

another.text: Pretend the paragraph is your friend telling you about their dog. Every sentence should be about the dog. If a new sentence is about what they ate for lunch, it doesn't belong, even if it's true.
another.example:
Story: My dog can open doors.
Fits: Last night he opened the fridge.
Doesn't fit: Dogs have 42 teeth.

steps.say: A sentence belongs only if it supports the paragraph's point. True and interesting is not enough.

steps.ask: Name the paragraph's point in a few words:
steps.then: Dams, ponds, homes for fish: all about changing rivers.

steps.ask: Add 'A single dam can flood several acres'? Does it help make that point?
options: Yes, flooding acres is reshaping a river

steps.ask: Add 'Beavers have orange teeth because of iron in the enamel'?
options: No: cool fact, nothing to do with rivers
steps.then: About beavers, yes. About reshaping rivers, no. Off-topic is off-topic even when true.
steps.hint: Check it against the point, not the animal.

questions.passage: Paragraph: The school's new schedule starts classes an hour later. Teachers report fewer students falling asleep, and attendance in first period has gone up.
questions.stem: Should the writer add: "Teenagers' bodies naturally want to sleep later than adults' do"?
options: Yes, it explains why the later start helps
No, it is about sleep rather than school
No, it repeats the first sentence
questions.why: The paragraph is about why a later start works. A sentence on teen sleep gives the reason.

questions.passage: Paragraph: The school's new schedule starts classes an hour later. Teachers report fewer students falling asleep, and attendance in first period has gone up.
questions.stem: Should the writer add: "The school was built in 1962"?
options: Yes, it gives background on the school
No, it has nothing to do with the schedule change
questions.why: True, but it doesn't help the point about the later start.

name: Should this sentence be deleted?
sub: Spotting the one that doesn't belong
rule: A sentence should be deleted if it wanders away from the paragraph's point, repeats something already said, or breaks the flow between its neighbors.
trick: Read the paragraph once with the sentence and once without it. If it reads better without, delete. If something is now missing, keep.
passage: Paragraph: (1) The city planted 400 trees downtown last year. (2) Trees cool the street by as much as ten degrees in summer. (3) My cousin lives downtown. (4) Shop owners say more people now linger on the shaded sidewalks.

examples.note: The cousin has nothing to do with the trees.
It explains why the trees matter. Without it, sentence 4 comes out of nowhere.

another.text: You're watching a show about sharks and suddenly there's a commercial about cereal. That jolt is what an off-topic sentence feels like. When a sentence makes you go "wait, what?", that's the one to delete. Read the paragraph without it to make sure.
another.example:
sharks → sharks → [cereal] → sharks
The cereal sentence goes.

steps.say: Delete a sentence if it wanders off the point, repeats something, or breaks the flow. Read the paragraph with it and without it.

options: The downtown trees and what they did

steps.ask: Sentence 3: 'My cousin lives downtown.' Does it help the point?
steps.then: 'Downtown' is a word match, not a point match.
steps.hint: What does the cousin have to do with the trees?

steps.ask: Sentence 2: 'Trees cool the street by ten degrees.' Read the paragraph without it. What happens?
options: Sentence 4's 'shaded sidewalks' comes out of nowhere
steps.then: Without it, something is missing. Keep it.

questions.passage: (1) Sourdough bread uses wild yeast instead of packaged yeast. (2) The wild yeast comes from a starter, a mix of flour and water that bakers feed for days. (3) Rye flour is darker than wheat flour. (4) That slow process is what gives sourdough its tangy taste.
questions.why: Rye versus wheat color has nothing to do with the sourdough process. Remove it and 2 flows straight into 4.

questions.passage: (1) The robotics club meets every Tuesday. (2) This year the team built a robot that sorts recycling. (3) It separates cans from bottles with a camera and a small arm. (4) The team built a robot that sorts recycling this year.
questions.why: Sentence 4 repeats sentence 2 almost word for word.

name: Topic sentences
sub: The sentence that tells you what's coming
rule: A topic sentence states the paragraph's main point up front. The best one covers everything the paragraph goes on to say, without being so broad it could start any paragraph.
trick: Read the body of the paragraph first. Then pick the opener that predicts it: not too narrow (only covers one detail), not too wide (covers the whole subject).
passage: Body: Its battery lasts two days. The camera works well in low light. And it costs a hundred dollars less than last year's model.

examples.text: The new phone improves on the old one in three ways.
The new phone has a better battery.
examples.note: Too narrow. Says nothing about camera or price.

another.text: A topic sentence is the title of a show. "Three gross things my dog does" tells you exactly what's coming. "Dogs exist" is too big. "My dog licks the floor" is too small when the paragraph lists three things. Pick the title that covers everything inside.
another.example:
Too big: Pets are interesting.
Too small: My dog licks the floor.
Just right: My dog does three gross things.

steps.say: A topic sentence predicts the paragraph. Read the body first, then pick the opener that covers all of it and nothing more.

steps.ask: The body mentions three things. Which three?
'The new phone has a better battery.' As an opener?
options: Too narrow: only one of the three
steps.then: It predicts the battery and nothing else.

steps.ask: 'Phones have changed a lot.' As an opener?
options: Too wide: it could start any paragraph
steps.then: True of everything, so it predicts nothing.

steps.ask: 'The new phone improves on the old one in three ways.'
options: Just right: it predicts all three
steps.then: Covers battery, camera and price, and promises exactly three. That is the fit.

questions.passage: Body: ___ Farmers lost most of the corn crop. Rivers dropped so low that barges could not move grain. In some towns, drinking water had to be trucked in.
options: The drought hurt the region in several ways.
questions.why: Crops, rivers, and drinking water are three kinds of drought damage. The first option is too narrow, the third too wide.

questions.passage: Body: ___ The old gym floor was replaced. The library got new shelves. Every classroom now has a projector.
options: The school replaced its gym floor.
The school made several upgrades over the summer.
questions.why: Gym, library, classrooms. "Several upgrades" covers all three.

name: From notes to a sentence
sub: Using only the notes that answer the goal
rule: When a question gives you notes and a goal, the right sentence uses the notes that serve the goal and leaves out the rest. Every choice is true; only one does the job.
trick: Underline the goal ("emphasize how fast," "compare the two," "introduce the topic to someone who has never heard of it"). Then check each choice against the goal alone.
passage:
Notes: The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889. It is 330 meters tall. It was built for a world's fair. It was meant to be taken down after 20 years.

Goal: Emphasize that the tower was not meant to be permanent.

examples.text: Built for an 1889 world's fair, the Eiffel Tower was meant to be taken down after 20 years.
The Eiffel Tower is 330 meters tall and was finished in 1889.
examples.note: True, but says nothing about being temporary.

another.text: You have a box of true facts about a tree. The question says "show how tall the tree is." Every answer uses true facts from the box, so nobody is lying. The right one uses the tall facts. It's not a truth test. It's a "did you do the job" test.
another.example:
Goal: show it's tall → use "300 feet"
Goal: show it's old → use "500 years old"

steps.say: Every choice is true. Only one does the job. So read the goal first and judge everything by it.

options: Emphasize that the tower was not meant to be permanent
Say how tall the tower is
steps.line: Goal: not meant to be permanent

options: Built for a fair, meant to come down after 20 years
steps.then: Height and date are true and useless here.
steps.hint: Which notes are about being temporary?

options: Built for an 1889 world's fair, the Eiffel Tower was meant to be taken down after 20 years.
The Eiffel Tower is 330 meters tall and was finished in 1889.
steps.then: The other one is true and says nothing about being temporary.
steps.line: ✓ 'meant to be taken down after 20 years'

questions.passage:
Notes: Hummingbirds weigh less than a nickel. They beat their wings up to 80 times a second. They can fly backward. They migrate up to 500 miles nonstop.

Goal: Emphasize how far hummingbirds can travel.
questions.stem: Which sentence best meets the goal?
options: Hummingbirds beat their wings up to 80 times a second.
Though they weigh less than a nickel, hummingbirds can migrate up to 500 miles nonstop.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backward.
questions.why: Only this one mentions distance. The nickel detail makes the 500 miles more impressive, which serves the goal.

questions.passage:
Notes: Composting turns food scraps into soil. It takes about three months. It keeps waste out of landfills. Landfill food waste produces methane, a greenhouse gas.

Goal: Explain why composting helps the environment.
questions.stem: Which sentence best meets the goal?
options: Composting keeps food scraps out of landfills, where they would produce methane, a greenhouse gas.
questions.why: Landfills, methane, greenhouse gas: that's the environmental reason. The others describe composting without saying why it helps.

name: Keep it on the goal
sub: The sentence that does what the question asks
rule: Some questions tell you what a sentence should accomplish: set up the next paragraph, give an example, acknowledge the other side. Pick the choice that does that specific job.
trick: Ignore which choice sounds nicest. Read the goal in the question, then ask of each choice: does it do exactly that?
passage:
Paragraph ends: ... so the new recycling bins were a success downtown.
Next paragraph begins: In the suburbs, however, the bins mostly sat empty.

examples.text: Goal: transition to the next paragraph. "Not every neighborhood saw the same result."

examples.note: True, but it doesn't set up the contrast coming next.

another.text: The question gives a job: "give an example" or "set up the next paragraph." It's a help-wanted sign. Four sentences show up. Three are perfectly nice but applied for the wrong job. Hire the one that does exactly what the sign says.
another.example:
Sign: give a specific example
Hire: "The library's recycling bin filled up twice a day."
Send home: "Recycling is important."

steps.say: Some questions give a sentence a job: set up the next paragraph, give an example, admit the other side. Ignore which choice sounds nicest.

steps.ask: This paragraph ends with the bins succeeding downtown. The next one begins 'In the suburbs, however, the bins sat empty.' The job is to transition. What must the sentence point at?
options: The contrast that is coming next
steps.line: Job: point toward the suburbs contrast

steps.ask: 'Recycling saves energy.' Does it do that job?
options: No: true, but it points nowhere

steps.ask: 'Not every neighborhood saw the same result.' Does it?
options: Yes, it sets up the suburbs
steps.then: It hands the reader to the next paragraph. That is the job.

questions.passage: The writer wants to acknowledge a possible objection before answering it. The paragraph argues the city should build more bike lanes.
questions.stem: Which choice best accomplishes the goal?
options: Bike lanes are good for the environment.
Some drivers worry that bike lanes will take away parking.
The city should start building right away.
questions.why: Naming the drivers' worry is acknowledging the other side. The others just continue the argument.

questions.passage: The paragraph has described how a volcano forms. The writer wants a sentence that transitions to the next paragraph, which is about how scientists predict eruptions.
questions.stem: Which choice best accomplishes the goal?
options: Knowing how a volcano forms is only half the job; the harder question is knowing when it will erupt.
questions.why: It closes the forming topic and opens the predicting topic in one move.
